content: Supported employment initiatives are specifically designed to improve vocational and economic inclusion for individuals with severe mental health conditions. These programs aim to quickly integrate individuals into paid employment while providing ongoing mental health and vocational support. This support is typically delivered through health, social, and employment services or psychosocial rehabilitation programs, enabling individuals to learn and adapt on the job. Reasonable accommodations in the workplace involve modifying the work environment to align with the worker's abilities, needs, and preferences. These accommodations are targeted interventions addressing barriers faced by individual workers rather than systemic organizational changes. Examples include flexible working hours, additional time to complete tasks, and time off for mental health care. Other accommodations may include access to private spaces for medication storage or rest, regular supportive meetings with supervisors, or job redesign to reduce client interaction if it causes undue stress. Return-to-work programs are structured to help workers re-enter and remain in employment following an absence due to mental health conditions. These programs often combine work-directed care, such as phased re-entry or reasonable accommodations, with evidence-based clinical care to support meaningful reintegration into the workplace while alleviating mental health symptoms. These interventions may also be necessary for workers caring for someone with a mental health condition. Both return-to-work programs and supported employment initiatives are multi-component interventions tailored to the individual worker. They involve collaboration among healthcare providers, employers, workers, and their representatives to identify and mobilize appropriate resources and strategies. Decisions about stakeholders and interventions should prioritize the worker's preferences, with regular reviews and adjustments to meet evolving support needs. Governments play a critical role in enabling these support interventions by ensuring employment laws align with international human rights standards. These laws should protect workers with mental health conditions from discrimination, address confidentiality, and provide reasonable accommodations and social protection. Employers are responsible for adhering to these rights-based laws, implementing non-discriminatory recruitment and employment practices, and consulting with workers and their representatives to address mental health and vocational support needs comprehensively. Employers must ensure workers are aware of available support options and protect the privacy of those seeking help. Anti-stigma measures are essential to counter misconceptions about mental health conditions, fostering an environment where individuals feel safe to seek support without fear of judgment or reprisal. These measures are cost-effective and critical for encouraging voluntary disclosure and access to support. Governments and employers should integrate mental health into occupational safety and health (OSH) management systems, ensuring a comprehensive approach to workplace mental health. This includes assigning senior leadership roles to champion mental health initiatives, securing sufficient funding, and embedding mental health into national OSH strategies. Policies and plans should be developed in consultation with workers, including those with lived experience of mental health conditions, to empower individuals in decisions about their mental health. Training for occupational and primary healthcare workers should include components on mental health, particularly workplace mental health. Mental health professionals should be equipped to supervise and support these providers in recognizing and addressing work-related mental health conditions. Strengthening national health systems is especially important in low-resource settings to ensure quality mental health services are accessible to all. Employers' and workers' organizations are key partners in improving workplace mental health. Their involvement in designing and implementing OSH policies fosters ownership and commitment, facilitating effective implementation. These organizations can raise awareness, provide training, and support the implementation of mental health regulations at the workplace level. They also play a critical role in addressing psychosocial risks and supporting workers affected by mental health concerns during discussions about sick leave, rehabilitation, or performance. Civil society, including non-governmental organizations and groups representing individuals with lived experience of mental health conditions, can significantly influence advocacy and action. Development partners may also contribute to implementation efforts in low-resource settings. Healthcare providers, particularly in primary care and occupational health, should be prepared to advise on and deliver interventions, supported by preand in-service training. Finally, governments, employers, and all stakeholders in the world of work must collaborate to improve mental health at work. This includes integrating mental health into national policies, conducting participatory research to understand risks and effective interventions, and ensuring compliance with evidence-based laws and regulations. A comprehensive, multi-stakeholder approach is essential to prevent, protect, promote, and support mental health in the workplace.
